title: Cybersecurity for Growing Businesses | CISO Global
summary: David Jemmett explains cybersecurity for growing businesses and what CEOs should review before new contracts, acquisitions, and AI rollouts.
body_markdown:
###### ***David Jemmett, Chief Executive Officer***


November 24, 2026


### “Security requirements belong in the budget and schedule we approve.”


Cybersecurity for growing businesses starts with the commitments we make to customers. Before we sign the next contract, I want to know whether we can meet them.


Everyone is focused on what the business just gained. Who is looking at what it now has to protect?


A larger customer can bring stricter security commitments. An acquisition can bring systems nobody has fully assessed. An AI tool can give employees a faster way to work while introducing a new path for sensitive information to leave the business.


Each decision can make commercial sense. The trouble starts when the company assumes its existing security arrangements will cover everything that comes next.


As a CEO, I want growth. I also want to know whether we can deliver what we just promised. That means putting cybersecurity into the conversation before the contract is signed, the systems are connected, or the AI tool becomes part of daily operations.


### The Contract Is Signed. Can You Keep the Promise?


Imagine winning your first customer that operates around the clock. Sales celebrates. Operations adds coverage. Your incident response agreement still assumes someone will investigate the next morning.


At 2 a.m., that gap becomes a customer problem.


The same applies to recovery commitments. If you promise to restore a critical service within four hours, when did you last demonstrate that you could? Does that test reflect the business you operate today?


Those answers affect contract economics, staffing, and customer trust. I want sales, operations, security, and legal to work through them together before we commit.


### Growth Changes the Consequences of a Failure


An application that once supported one office may now process orders for the entire company. The software has not changed. The financial impact of losing it has.


An acquisition creates a similar challenge. Ownership can change in a day. Understanding inherited access, vendors, and recovery arrangements takes longer.


Before connecting the businesses, ask what has actually been assessed, what remains unknown, and who is responsible during the transition. If a departing provider holds the knowledge needed to restore a system, that belongs on the integration agenda.


### AI Belongs in the Growth Conversation


AI can help a growing team handle more work. I want our people exploring that opportunity. I also want us to understand what we are authorizing.


Consider an employee using an AI assistant to summarize a customer agreement. Which tool are they using? Is confidential information permitted there? What do the provider’s terms and settings allow it to retain or use?


Now consider an AI agent connected to email, customer records, or internal systems. The review needs to cover what it can access, what it can change, and which actions require human approval. A tool that drafts a response needs different permissions from one that can send it or update a customer record.


Start with a defined business purpose. Approve the tool and the data it may use. Limit access to what the task requires. Decide who reviews consequential outputs, and make sure someone can stop the workflow if it behaves unexpectedly.


AI adoption should have an accountable business owner and a practical fallback if the service becomes unavailable. Those responsibilities need to be settled before the team depends on it.


### The Cost of Cybersecurity for Growing Businesses


If a new customer requires stronger access controls, budget for them. If expansion requires continuous monitoring and response, confirm the coverage. If an AI workflow needs testing, staff training, and ongoing oversight, include that work in the business case.


Leaving those costs out makes the opportunity look more profitable than it is. It also puts teams under pressure to accept unfinished work because a launch date has already been promised.


Security requirements belong in the budget and schedule we approve. Discovering them just before launch leaves everyone with fewer choices.


### Go Back After Launch and Ask What Remains Open


Temporary access can become permanent. An acquired system can remain in use long after its planned retirement. An approved AI pilot can expand into workflows nobody reviewed.


Set a review date when approving the initiative. Ask the responsible executive to explain what remains unfinished, what exposure it creates, and when it will be resolved.


At your next leadership meeting, choose one recent contract, acquisition, or AI rollout. Ask this question:


**What are we relying on today that our security and recovery plans have not caught up with?**
